title: Parents Should Not Feel Guilty for Choosing a Good School
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman responds to Nikole Hannah-Jones's widely discussed New York Times essay about sending her daughter to a struggling, majority-Black New York City school out of a commitment to integration. Rather than relitigate the whole essay, he curates and extends reactions from Anna Stokke, Andrew Rotherham, John Arnold, Daniel Willingham, Derrell Bradford and others. His central argument is that the story exposes the danger of ignoring the gap between good grades and actual proficiency, since the daughter's math gaps surfaced only when selective high school admissions arrived. He also presses the question of accountability, noting that the school spent heavily per student yet posted dismal attendance and math results. The piece closes by challenging the moral framework of school choice debates: parents should not be asked to sacrifice their own children's interests for a policy ideal, and personal convictions should not be turned into obligations for other families.
points: Aldeman highlights that the daughter earned good grades and loved math while failing to reach proficiency on the state test, a warning sign her parents dismissed as being bad at tests.
The school Hannah-Jones chose spent roughly $52K per student yet had 57% chronic absenteeism and only 23% math proficiency, undercutting a resource-shortage explanation.
Drawing on Daniel Willingham, he argues that a strong family background can soften but never fully replace good instruction.
He endorses Derrell Bradford's principle that public policy should not require parents to act against their own children's best interests.
quotes: While she was getting good grades and even said math was her favorite subject, she wasn't scoring proficient on the state test. Hannah-Jones dismissed this as her being "bad at tests," but eventually discovered that her daughter hadn't mastered long division and fractions.
When kids have math gaps, they might be ok in the short run if they're still getting good grades. But math gaps have a way of showing up later in different, consequential ways.
despite these resources the school had a chronic absenteeism rate of 57%, and just 23% of its students were proficient in math. To put it mildly, those are awful results.
But Daniel Willingham notes that this story is a reminder that good family background can mitigate bad schooling somewhat, but it can't fully substitute for good instruction.
Hannah-Jones' original theory of action depended on parents like her choosing struggling, high-poverty schools rather than fleeing them.

She believed deeply in integration and in the importance of families like hers committing themselves to public schools serving disadvantaged children. She didn't merely tell other people to make a sacrifice she was unwilling to make herself.
For years, Hannah-Jones has been part of a conversation about school choice that attaches moral significance to where parents send their children. But parents shouldn't have to carry that burden.
